2.text: district, in order to avoid influenza, coming as usual from the west, retreated

3.text: for several days’ journey from the nearest camp of the western people on

4.text: the head waters of the Anui.

5.text: While a contagious disease is raging, the “shunning” of everybody

6.text: suspected of being followed by the “spirit” is carried to the greatest extent.

7.text: Even a visit to a camp tainted by disease is considered as a kind of

8.text: trespass, a desire to tempt the keˊlᴇ, who otherwise might have passed by

10.text: According to an account by Aiñanwaˊt, during the small-pox epidemic

11.text: of 1884, some sick people, while still alive, were left by their house-mates,

12.text: who tried to flee from the anger of the keˊlᴇ. At the same time, some of

13.text: the camps which stood quite apart escaped unharmed. One Aˊmčê, a rich

14.text: reindeer-breeder, lived with many daughters, all of whom were married. One

15.text: of his sons-in-law, also a well-to-do breeder, lived by himself. His camp was

16.text: visited by the keˊlᴇ; and all the family, except the daughter of Aˊmčê and

17.text: one young boy, died. These two had fled to a neighboring camp, leaving

18.text: the husband dangerously ill. After a while the woman was visited by her

19.text: father, who took her to his own camp.

20.text: The disease passed over, and the people began to live without fear.

21.text: Then Aˊmčê thought about his son-in-law. They both were shamans, and

22.text: Aˊmčê argued that the other might have escaped, after all. At last he resolved

23.text: to visit the stricken camp. They started, a party of five, two other sons-in-law

24.text: of Aˊmčê being of the number. When they reached the camp, Aˊmčê,

25.text: brandishing his spear, went toward the tent of his daughter, and ripped the

26.text: wall, taking care not to touch it with his bare hands. This is one of the

27.text: usual precautions against contact with the “spirits.” After that, Aˊmčê ripped

28.text: also a wall of the inner room, and saw the corpse of his son-in-law. “Oh!”

29.text: said he, “then you are really dead. What can I do for you? It is of no

30.text: use to carry you into the wilderness. You have here the whole tent at your

31.text: command. Well, I have seen you, at least. Good-by! I am going.”

32.text: When they reached home, however, the two sons-in-law of Aˊmčê who

33.text: had been of the party suddenly grew ill and died. Two others fled from

34.text: the camp and thus saved their lives. But none of Aˊmčê’s own offspring

36.text: The narrator told all this, attaching the greatest blame to Aˊmčê for his

37.text: conduct, who acted as though he desired to find a keˊlᴇ and draw him to

38.text: his own place. The explanation offered by the teller of the story as being

39.text: the possible one was, that Aˊmčê, being a shaman, foresaw some bad luck

40.text: for his family, and wanted to sacrifice to the keˊlet the people of “alien

41.text: blood,” though they were his sons-in-law.¹
